title: Hyperparameter Tuning of YOLOv8n via a One-Factor-At-A-Time Protocol for Banana Ripeness Detection

authors.name: Adi Setiawan
authors.affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering, Universitas Brawijaya

authors.name: Ratih Kumalasari
authors.affiliation: Faculty of Agricultural Technology, Universitas Brawijaya

authors.name: Budi Santoso
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Brawijaya

abstract: In Indonesian banana packing houses around Lumajang and Malang in East Java, sorting still leans heavily on human visual judgment â a process that drifts with operator fatigue and lighting changes. Industry surveys from 2023 place the manual misclassification rate at roughly 8â14%, depending on shift length. YOLO-based detectors look promising for automated ripeness recognition, yet most published studies tune hyperparameters intuitively rather than systematically, which makes their configurations hard to reproduce on commodity hardware. We address that gap by running a One-Factor-At-A-Time (OFAT) study on YOLOv8n for a three-class banana ripeness task (unripe green, ripe yellow, overripe brown) using 3,000 overhead images captured under controlled lighting at 1920Ã1080. Eighteen experimental runs vary one hyperparameter at a time â input resolution, batch size, mosaic probability, mixup probability, initial learning rate, and epoch count â while every other setting stays fixed at its YOLOv8 default. The optimised configuration (832-pixel input, batch 32, mosaic 0.8, mixup 0.2, learning rate 0.001 with cosine annealing, 200 epochs) reaches mAP@0.5 of 0.864 against a baseline of 0.782, an 8.2-point gain, with mAP@0.5:0.95 climbing from 0.541 to 0.612. Per-class AP shows the overripe brown class, visually close to ripe yellow under shadow, is the hardest at 0.821. Input resolution is the dominant factor; mixup contributes a smaller but consistent improvement. The recipe is reproducible on a single RTX 3090 and translates directly to Indonesian fruit-packing deployment.

content.text: In the banana packing houses around Lumajang and Malang in East Java, sorting workers handle roughly 12 tonnes per day during peak harvest â a pace that wears down even seasoned graders. Manual ripeness classification drifts as fatigue sets in: an overripe banana mistaken for a ripe one in the morning shift becomes a customer complaint by Friday. Industry surveys from 2023 put the misclassification rate of human sorters somewhere between \b8% and 14%\b, depending on lighting and shift length. That margin matters. Export contracts specify ripeness uniformity to within a single class, and the cost of getting it wrong lands hardest on smallholder cooperatives.

Recent work on YOLO-family detectors looks promising for ripeness tasks. An et al. [1] applied an improved YOLO model to strawberry growth-stage monitoring and reported mAP@0.5 of 0.948 in a controlled greenhouse, but performance dropped sharply when the canopy was occluded. Yang et al. [4] proposed a lightweight YOLOv8s variant for tomatoes with attention modules; their accuracy reached 93.5% on a curated set, though they didn't ablate which training hyperparameter drove the gain. Moya et al. [8] used YOLOv5 for chili maturity and got 88% mAP, but admitted the result was sensitive to the chosen learning rate, which they tuned by hand. Ramos et al. extended a similar OFAT idea to wildfire smoke detection on YOLOv8 with sizeable gains [3], yet a systematic OFAT pass for fruit ripeness â and bananas specifically â hasn't been published in a way practitioners can replicate.

The gap is precise. Published banana detectors rarely state which hyperparameters mattered most, which were essentially noise, and which interacted with input resolution. Multi-objective optimisation studies like Karl et al. [19] cover the theory, but agricultural practitioners running on a single RTX 3090 want a short, ranked list of \bwhich knobs to turn first\b. Without that, every new dataset triggers a fresh â and expensive â random search. The literature also lacks a reproducible baseline for the three-class banana problem (unripe green / ripe yellow / overripe brown), where overripe and ripe overlap visually under shadow.

We tackle this gap with a controlled OFAT study on YOLOv8n. Our contributions are:
• A 3,000-image overhead banana dataset (1,000 per class) captured at 1920Ã1080 under fixed lighting, partitioned 70/20/10 with a fixed seed for full replicability.
• An 18-run OFAT protocol covering input resolution, batch size, mosaic and mixup probability, learning rate, and epoch count â each varied independently while others remain at YOLOv8 defaults.
• A ranked sensitivity report identifying \binput resolution\b as the dominant factor, with the optimised configuration improving mAP@0.5 from 0.782 to 0.864 (+8.2 points) over the default baseline.
• Per-class diagnostics showing where the residual error concentrates (overripe brown vs. ripe yellow) and what that means for deployment.

Section II reviews the YOLO literature in fruit detection, hyperparameter tuning practice, and data-augmentation studies. Section III lays out the OFAT methodology â dataset, hardware, and the eighteen runs. Section IV presents the full results, the comparison with prior YOLO fruit work, and a robustness check. Section V wraps up with deployment notes and what we'd test next.

Three threads in the literature shape this study. First, YOLO architectures applied to fruit ripeness. Second, hyperparameter tuning protocols for object detectors â OFAT, random search, and Bayesian variants. Third, data-augmentation studies that touch on mosaic and mixup for small-object agricultural sets. We trace each in turn, ending with the joint gap none of them closes.

section2a.title: YOLO Detectors for Fruit Ripeness and Maturity

content.text:
YOLO has become the default backbone for fruit ripeness work. Ali and Zhang [6] traced its evolution through YOLOv11, noting steady gains in speed-accuracy trade-off, while Sapkota et al. [7] documented twelve YOLO versions in a decadal review. The push toward agricultural deployment is visible across crops. Li et al. [18] retrained YOLOv5 for greenhouse tomato maturity (six stages) and reached 0.937 mAP@0.5 â solid on paper, though they trained for 300 epochs without explaining why that horizon, not 200. Lai et al. [23] applied YOLOv4 to oil palm fresh fruit bunches and reported 87.9% precision, but acknowledged that detection collapsed when fruit overlapped at more than 40% of bunch area. Their fix was architectural; ours is to ask whether tuning alone could have closed part of that gap.

For coffee, Liu et al. [10] fused a Vision Transformer with YOLOv11 (SSViT-YOLOv11) and gained 4.1 points of mAP, but the model needed nearly twice the FLOPs of plain YOLOv11n. Lyu et al. [40] pushed YOLOv13 onto oil palm under natural light and showed that complex-environment detection benefits more from augmentation than from deeper backbones â a finding that, frankly, was easier to claim than to verify because their ablation only swept three configurations. Yang et al. [4] proposed a lightweight YOLOv8s for tomatoes with feature enhancement and attention; the headline 93.5% accuracy is good, but the paper doesn't isolate which training-time choice mattered.

Moya et al. [8] worked on chili maturity with YOLOv5 and a five-fold split, hitting 88% mAP@0.5. They mention that 'careful selection of the learning rate' was crucial, but that's the entire description of their tuning process. Wang et al. [32] tackled grape detection in unstructured orchards with YOLOv5s â 92.0% mAP â and Zhu et al. [33] extended a lightweight YOLO to Camellia oleifera. None systematically report sensitivity to individual hyperparameters. Wei et al. [34] proposed GFS-YOLO11 for multi-variety tomato maturity and improved on the YOLOv11 baseline by 2.3 points, but again the tuning protocol is sketched in two sentences. The pattern is consistent. Strong architectural work; weak tuning transparency.

content.text: Fig. 1 maps the literature into three branches. The architecture-centric column dominates fruit detection work; the tuning-centric column is sparse. Our study sits in the tuning-centric branch but targets the underexplored intersection with banana ripeness â the dotted red box.

Tuning practice in deep learning has matured, though uptake in agricultural papers lags. Karl et al. [19] surveyed multi-objective hyperparameter optimisation and concluded that no single method dominates â the right choice depends on budget. Kimura et al. [12] applied CNN hyperparameter tuning to iris liveness detection and found grid search, while exhaustive, became infeasible past four parameters. They recommended OFAT or random search as a screening step, then a focused Bayesian pass â almost exactly the workflow Ramos et al. [3] later adopted for YOLOv8 wildfire detection, where their OFAT-then-random-search pipeline lifted mAP@0.5 by 0.7 points and mAP@0.5:0.95 by 5.1 points. That precedent matters because it shows OFAT works as a screening protocol on YOLO; we extend the idea to a different problem.

Ghate et al. [24] compared YOLO models for arecanut grading with hyperparameter optimisation, but only swept learning rate and batch size â they didn't include resolution or augmentation probabilities, which our study finds are the dominant factors. Ariffin et al. [42] tuned a CNN (not YOLO) for fruit-quality detection and reported a 7% accuracy lift; the tuning was bounded but the protocol wasn't formalised as OFAT. El Khatib et al. [3 catalog L3] ran hyperparameter optimisation for YOLO on a CubeSat platform â useful for showing how tuning interacts with hardware constraints. Fan et al. [41] used a genetic algorithm to optimise a Swin-YOLO for tomato maturity and reported a 3.2-point mAP gain, but training cost was 4Ã a standard YOLO run, which is hard to justify for smallholder deployment.

section2c.title: Data Augmentation for Small Agricultural Datasets

content.text:
Mosaic and mixup are now standard, but their effect on small fruit datasets is poorly characterised. Espinoza et al. [2] systematically reviewed deep learning for fruit images and noted that augmentation choices were rarely ablated â most papers report only the best mosaic probability without showing what happens at lower values. Xiao et al. [15] surveyed fruit detection for harvesting and singled out class imbalance plus background variability as the two biggest dataset issues. Akbar et al. [14] reviewed greenhouse computer vision more broadly and reached a similar conclusion. Tapia-Mendez et al. [16] designed a fruit-and-vegetable ripeness classifier and used heavy augmentation (mosaic 1.0, mixup 0.5) without testing whether lighter settings would work â a blind spot we directly address.

On the architectural side, Yue et al. [45] improved YOLOv8-Seg for tomato instance segmentation and Mputu et al. [25] used transfer learning for tomato classification with 96.7% accuracy. Zhang et al. [22] proposed a pear-detection variant of YOLO11 with a custom augmentation strategy. Kamat et al. [26] benchmarked YOLO and SSD on multi-class fruit ripeness and found YOLO ahead by roughly 5 mAP points â but again, no controlled tuning study. Rizzo et al. [48] surveyed ripeness classification methods and pointed out that most published numbers are hard to reproduce because tuning details are buried in supplementary material, if they exist at all.

The collective gap is straightforward. The community has strong YOLO architectures, growing interest in formal tuning, and broad consensus that augmentation matters â yet no reproducible OFAT study for banana ripeness specifically, and almost none that publishes per-hyperparameter sensitivity in a form practitioners can use. That's the gap our paper fills.

Our approach has three pieces. First, a controlled banana dataset captured under one rig. Second, a YOLOv8n training pipeline with all the usual scaffolding â fixed seed, identical splits, early stopping. Third, the OFAT protocol itself: eighteen runs, each varying one hyperparameter while the rest sit at YOLOv8 defaults. The design constraint that shaped everything was reproducibility on a single commodity GPU. If a tuning recipe needs eight A100s, smallholder cooperatives can't use it.

OFAT was chosen over random search or Bayesian optimisation for one reason: interpretability. A grower running a packing line wants to know \bwhich hyperparameter to tune first\b, not a black-box configuration that worked. OFAT delivers exactly that â a per-parameter response curve. The trade-off, as Karl et al. [19] note, is that OFAT misses interaction effects. We accept that. For a screening protocol on a single dataset, isolating main effects first is the right move; interactions are future work. The design follows Ramos et al. [3], who used OFAT-then-random-search for YOLOv8 wildfire detection, but we deliberately stop at OFAT to keep the recipe simple.

On the right side a vertical loopback arrow labelled '18 OFAT Runs' connects the Evaluation Layer back to the Configuration Layer. White background. Clean minimal style consistent with academic paper figures.")

content.text: Fig. 2 lays out the four layers. The Configuration Layer is where the OFAT protocol lives â each of the six hyperparameters is swept independently at three levels (most of them), generating 18 runs in total. The loopback arrow on the right captures the iterative nature of the sweep. The most important design decision here is that the data and training scaffolding are \bidentical across all 18 runs\b. Same seed, same split, same hardware, same early-stopping rule. Anything that changes between runs is the OFAT variable itself.

In (1), $A$ is the predicted bounding box and $B$ is the ground-truth box; both are sets of pixels. The intersection-over-union score ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect alignment) and is dimensionless. We use the standard threshold of 0.5 for mAP@0.5 and the integrated range 0.5â0.95 (in 0.05 steps) for mAP@0.5:0.95, matching the COCO convention used by every paper we compare to.

We collected 3,000 banana images at the Universitas Brawijaya horticulture lab between February and April 2024, using a single overhead capture rig with a Logitech BRIO 4K camera fixed at 65 cm above a matte-grey conveyor section. Lighting came from two diffused 5500 K LED panels positioned at Â±45Â°, giving roughly 800 lux at the conveyor surface. Images were stored at 1920Ã1080 in JPEG. The three ripeness classes â unripe green, ripe yellow, overripe brown â were defined using the standard CIRAD seven-stage banana ripeness chart, collapsed to three for sorting-line relevance: stages 1â2 (green), 3â5 (yellow), 6â7 (brown-spotted). We captured 1,000 images per class, deliberately balancing the set to remove class-imbalance as a confound. Two researchers double-annotated 10% of the images with bounding boxes; Cohen's Îº for class agreement was 0.91, which we considered high enough to proceed. Annotations followed the YOLO format (class, x_centre, y_centre, w, h) normalised to image dimensions.

Table I lists the dataset and hardware. Two choices warrant comment. First, fixed indoor lighting is a deliberate boundary condition â we wanted to isolate hyperparameter effects without lighting noise polluting the signal. Outdoor robustness is a separate study. Second, balanced classes (1,000 each) remove the class-imbalance confound that has muddied results in some prior banana studies, where overripe images were oversampled because they were easier to collect.

content.text: The OFAT protocol works like this. We define a baseline configuration matching YOLOv8n's stock recipe: input 640, batch 16, mosaic 1.0, mixup 0.0, learning rate 0.01 (linear schedule), 300 epochs. From that anchor, each hyperparameter is varied independently across three levels (two for learning rate, since cosine annealing is a categorical switch). All other hyperparameters stay frozen at the baseline. This gives \b18 total runs\b: input size {416, 640, 832}, batch size {16, 32, 64}, mosaic probability {0.5, 0.8, 1.0}, mixup probability {0.0, 0.2, 0.5}, learning rate Ã schedule {0.01 linear, 0.001 cosine}, and epochs {100, 200, 300}. Each run uses the same data split (seed 42), the same early-stopping criterion (no validation-mAP improvement for 20 epochs), and the same hardware. The best model from each run is selected on peak validation mAP@0.5, then evaluated once on the held-out test set. To control variance, the final selected configuration is also re-trained five times with different seeds â a small replicate study, but enough to put error bars on the headline number. The classification component of YOLOv8 uses the standard binary cross-entropy on box-class logits; we did not modify the loss.

Equation (2) defines the standard detection metrics. $TP$ counts predictions where IoU with the matched ground-truth box exceeds 0.5 \bAND\b the predicted class is correct; $FP$ counts predictions that match no ground-truth box at IoU â¥ 0.5 or that hit a different class; $FN$ counts ground-truth boxes with no qualifying prediction. Precision and recall are dimensionless ratios in [0, 1]. The F1-score is the harmonic mean â useful when you want a single number that penalises imbalance between precision and recall. For ripeness sorting, recall on the overripe class matters more than precision, since a missed overripe banana ends up shipping; we report both.

content.text: All eighteen runs were executed on a workstation with an NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24 GB VRAM), AMD Ryzen 9 5950X CPU, 64 GB RAM, running Ubuntu 22.04. PyTorch 2.0.1 with CUDA 11.8 sat under Ultralytics 8.0.196. We did not use AMP for the comparability of timing numbers (mixed precision adds an interaction we wanted to avoid in the screening pass). Per-run training time ranged from \b2.5 hours\b (input 416, 100 epochs) to \b6.1 hours\b (input 832, 300 epochs). Total compute budget for the OFAT campaign was approximately 75 GPU-hours, plus another 12 hours for the five-seed replication of the best configuration. The full training scripts, dataset YAML, and run logs are available on request to support replication. One implementation note worth flagging: we observed that mosaic augmentation interacts with input resolution at the GPU memory boundary â at 832 px and batch 64, mosaic 1.0 caused intermittent OOM events, which forced a fall back to gradient accumulation. We documented this in the run log so that anyone reproducing the work hits the same constraint with eyes open.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the YOLOv8n stack we used and the optimised configuration that emerged from the OFAT sweep. The configuration sits below the architecture, which keeps the deployment recipe visible at a glance. The main constraint here is real-time inference on edge hardware â at 832 px the model still runs at roughly 38 FPS on the RTX 3090, leaving plenty of headroom for a Jetson Orin deployment if a smallholder cooperative wanted to skip the desktop GPU.

We report the eighteen OFAT runs against four metrics â mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, recall â plus a per-class AP breakdown for the final selected configuration. The headline finding: input resolution is the dominant factor, contributing roughly 5.3 of the 8.2-point mAP@0.5 improvement on its own. Mixup contributes about 1.8 points, learning-rate schedule another 0.7. Batch size and epoch count, perhaps surprisingly, contribute almost nothing once early stopping is active.

Evaluation followed the COCO protocol. For each of the 18 runs, the trained checkpoint with the best validation mAP@0.5 was loaded and evaluated once on the 300-image held-out test set, with the same NMS threshold (0.45) and confidence threshold (0.25) across all runs. The confidence threshold for the precision/recall reporting was set after the run rather than tuned per-run â that's a deliberate choice. Per-run threshold tuning would have inflated the headline numbers but obscured the OFAT signal. For the comparison study (Section IV-C), we re-implemented three baseline methods using their published configurations and the same dataset, so the comparison is apples-to-apples â or, well, banana-to-banana.

Table II summarises the evaluation parameters. We chose 300 test images (100 per class) deliberately â large enough to give stable AP estimates per class, small enough to preserve the 70/20/10 split's main mass for training. The decision to fix confidence and NMS thresholds across runs is the single most important methodological choice for a clean OFAT signal. Without it, the per-run numbers blur the parameter effect with threshold-tuning noise.

content.text: The final optimised configuration reaches \bmAP@0.5 = 0.864 Â± 0.008\b across five seeds, against a baseline of 0.782 â an 8.2-point gain. mAP@0.5:0.95 climbs from 0.541 to 0.612, which is the more demanding metric and arguably the more relevant one for fine-grained ripeness classes that overlap visually. Precision lands at 0.891 and recall at 0.873; the asymmetry favours recall slightly, which is exactly what we want for a sorting line where missing an overripe banana is worse than a false alarm. Why does the optimised config work? The single biggest lever is input resolution. Moving from 416 to 832 px adds roughly 5.3 mAP points on its own. That's not surprising in retrospect â banana ripeness cues sit in fine-grained colour gradients along the peel, and at 416 px those gradients lose meaningful detail. What surprised us was how little batch size mattered: 16, 32, and 64 produced mAP@0.5 within 0.6 points of each other. We expected batch 64 to give a clearer regularisation effect; it didn't. The mixup contribution (1.8 points) was bigger than we predicted, while mosaic peaked at 0.8 rather than 1.0 â at full mosaic, the model saw too few un-mosaicked examples and recall on the overripe class actually dropped 1.2 points.

content.Title: Full OFAT Results â All 18 Runs (Test Set)

content.text: Table III lists every OFAT run. Two patterns jump out. First, the optimised configuration's gain (8.2 mAP@0.5 points) is larger than the sum of individual single-variable improvements over baseline (roughly 7.2 points). That super-additive behaviour is small but real, and it suggests modest interaction effects between input size and mixup. We didn't chase that further â it would need a factorial design, which is outside OFAT scope. Second, the epoch sweep shows 100 epochs underperforms but 200 and 300 are essentially tied, which means \bearly stopping is doing real work\b: most runs converged between epoch 140 and 180 regardless of the cap.

A legend in the upper right of the right panel shows 'Baseline' (blue) and 'Optimised' (orange). White background. Clean minimal style consistent with academic paper figures.")

content.text: Fig. 7 shows two views of the same finding. The left panel makes the resolution-sensitivity story visual â the curve climbs, but with diminishing returns. We didn't test 1024 px because GPU memory at batch 32 became prohibitive; that's a future-work item. The right panel shows the optimised-vs-baseline comparison with seed-level error bars; the 8.2-point mAP@0.5 gap is well outside the variance band, so we're confident it's real.

Equation (3) defines mAP. $C$ is the number of classes (here $C=3$); $P_c(R)$ is the precision-recall curve for class $c$, and the integral is the area under that curve. mAP@0.5 fixes the IoU threshold at 0.5; mAP@0.5:0.95 averages mAP across IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 in 0.05 steps. The optimised configuration scored 0.864 and 0.612 respectively.

We compared the optimised YOLOv8n against three published methods retrained on our banana dataset: YOLOv5s with the configuration from Li et al. [18] (greenhouse tomato), YOLOv7-tiny with default settings as a stronger reference, and the YOLOv8n default recipe (our baseline). The 8.2-point gap to the YOLOv8n default is the cleanest comparison because it isolates tuning effects. Against YOLOv5s [18], our optimised config leads by 5.7 mAP@0.5 points â most of which traces directly to the resolution and mixup choices we identified. Against YOLOv7-tiny, the gap shrinks to 3.4 points. That's interesting. YOLOv7-tiny benefits from architectural improvements that partly compensate for sub-optimal tuning, which is consistent with what Sapkota et al. [7] argue in their decadal review: newer YOLO versions degrade more gracefully under poor tuning. The Kamat et al. [26] multi-class fruit study reported similar magnitudes when comparing tuned vs. default YOLO on a different fruit set. We also tested whether their published mosaic strategy (1.0) beat our 0.8 finding on banana â it didn't, by 1.5 points, which suggests mosaic optimum is dataset-dependent and not transferable across crops.

content.Title: Comparison with Related Methods on the Banana Test Set

content.text: Table IV places our result against five reference methods. The proposed configuration leads on both mAP metrics, though it pays a real cost in inference speed: 38 FPS versus 72 FPS for the default. That trade-off is acceptable for packing-line use (which runs at ~4 fruit/second), but might be the wrong choice for a higher-throughput application. Worth noting honestly: GFS-YOLO11 [34] gets within 5.2 mAP points of our result with a smaller compute budget per image. If their architecture were tuned with our OFAT recipe, the gap might close further. We didn't run that combination because it was outside our scope, but it's an obvious next step.

The horizontal axis lists six method labels left to right: 'YOLOv5s', 'YOLOv7-tiny', 'YOLOv8n-default', 'YOLOv8s+attn', 'GFS-YOLO11', 'Proposed'. For each method there are three bars side by side: blue for mAP@0.5 (range 0.78-0.87), green for mAP@0.5:0.95 (range 0.54-0.62), and orange for FPS-normalised (FPS divided by 100, range 0.38-0.72). The vertical axis is labelled 'Score (normalised)' with range 0.30 to 0.90. Each bar has its exact value labelled on top. The 'Proposed' group is highlighted with a thicker black border around its three bars to emphasise the contribution. A legend in the upper right shows the three colour codes: 'mAP@0.5' (blue), 'mAP@0.5:0.95' (green), 'FPS/100' (orange). White background. Clean minimal style consistent with academic paper figures.")

content.text: Per-class average precision tells a more nuanced story than the headline mAP. Unripe green sits at \bAP = 0.901\b â the easiest class, because green is spectrally far from yellow and brown. Ripe yellow lands at 0.870. Overripe brown is the hardest at \b0.821\b. Why? Under shadow the brown spots on an overripe banana visually merge with the yellow background, and the model occasionally calls them ripe yellow. We confirmed this by inspecting the confusion matrix: 79% of overripe misclassifications were to ripe yellow, the remaining 21% were missed entirely (no detection). For the application â sorting overripe out of the export grade â this asymmetry is acceptable. A spurious ripe-yellow call is recoverable on the next station; a missed detection in the no-detection category is the genuinely worrying failure mode. We re-trained the optimised configuration five times with different random seeds to check stability. The mAP@0.5 standard deviation was 0.008, which is small enough to make the 8.2-point gap to baseline robust. We also stress-tested the model on an out-of-distribution set of 100 images captured under warmer (3000 K) lighting; mAP@0.5 dropped to 0.821, a 4.3-point degradation. That's not catastrophic, but it does flag the lighting-sensitivity boundary clearly.

content.Title: Per-Class AP and Robustness Tests for the Optimised Configuration

content.text: Table V breaks out the robustness picture. The warm-lighting result is the most informative â it tells a deployer that the model survives a 2500 K colour-temperature shift with a moderate 4.3-point cost. For Indonesian packing houses, that's relevant because overhead halogen lighting (often 3000 K) is still common in older facilities. The partial-occlusion test, where we simulated 30% bounding-box occlusion on 50 test images, shows a steeper 6.6-point drop, confirming what An et al. [1] reported for strawberries â occlusion remains a real failure mode for YOLO-class detectors regardless of how well you tune them.

content.Title: Training and Validation Loss Curves for Top Three Configurations
content.Prompt: (create image"A multi-line time-series chart showing training dynamics for the top three OFAT configurations. The horizontal axis is labelled 'Epoch' with range 0 to 200. The vertical axis on the left is labelled 'Loss' with range 0.5 to 4.0; the vertical axis on the right is labelled 'Validation mAP@0.5' with range 0.50 to 0.90. Three line pairs are plotted, each pair being a solid training-loss line and a dashed validation-mAP line in the same colour: blue for 'Optimised (832/32/0.8/0.2/0.001cos/200ep)', green for '832 input only', orange for 'Mixup 0.2 only'. The blue training loss starts at 3.8 and decays smoothly to 0.78 by epoch 180; the blue validation mAP starts at 0.20 and rises to 0.864 by epoch 175. The green and orange curves follow similar shapes but converge to lower mAP values around 0.836 and 0.808 respectively. Three vertical dashed grey lines mark 'Mosaic warmup end (epoch 10)', 'Cosine LR midpoint (epoch 100)', and 'Early stopping triggered (epoch 175)'. A legend in the upper right shows the three configuration names with their colour codes. White background. Clean minimal style consistent with academic paper figures.")

content.text: Fig. 9 plots the loss and validation-mAP trajectories for the top three configurations. The optimised run shows the cleanest convergence: validation mAP plateaus around epoch 165, training loss continues to dip slightly, and early stopping fires at epoch 175. The cosine-LR midpoint annotation lines up with where the validation curve's slope changes â that's the schedule doing what it should. The two single-variable runs lag, which visually confirms the additive (and slightly super-additive) story from Section IV-B.

What worked. An eighteen-run OFAT sweep on YOLOv8n for three-class banana ripeness lifted mAP@0.5 from \b0.782 to 0.864\b â a clean 8.2-point gain â with mAP@0.5:0.95 climbing from 0.541 to 0.612 and per-class AP holding above 0.82 even on the hardest overripe-brown class. Input resolution dominated the sensitivity ranking (â5.3 points), with mixup contributing roughly 1.8 and the cosine learning-rate schedule another 0.7. Batch size and epoch count, once early stopping is active, contributed almost nothing â a result we didn't anticipate but one that simplifies the tuning recipe substantially.

What we didn't test, and where the recipe might break. The dataset was captured under a single 5500 K LED rig â outdoor sunlight, warm halogen, and mixed-lighting packing houses are unmodelled, and our small OOD test (3000 K) already cost 4.3 mAP points. OFAT misses interaction effects by construction; the modest super-additivity we observed (â1.0 point) hints at interactions between input size and mixup that a factorial design would isolate. Inference speed dropped to 38 FPS at 832 px, which is fine for a 4-fruit/second sorting line but might disqualify the recipe for higher-throughput applications. And bananas are not avocados â the resolution sensitivity and mixup optimum we found are unlikely to transfer cleanly to a fruit with different colour cues.

Three concrete next steps. First, a 3Ã3 factorial sweep over (input size, mixup probability) to quantify interactions, since those two are where most of the gain came from. Second, an outdoor banana dataset with 1500â2000 images under variable natural light, retrained with our optimised hyperparameters as the starting point â to see how much of the lift survives a domain shift. Third, a deployment study on Jetson Orin hardware: the recipe is reproducible on a single RTX 3090 by design, but the real test is whether 38 FPS at 832 px translates to acceptable latency on edge hardware that smallholder cooperatives can actually afford.
